final_answer:
Short answer: whichever single office can validly bring ALL of the doctor's false claims (both states) in one indictment should do so, and that choice matters more than which state it is. Under the Guidelines, the two offices cannot be played off against each other for a higher total: a consolidated prosecution gives the longest exposure, while split prosecutions tend to collapse into concurrent time. If only one office has venue over all the conduct, that office should indict. If both do (or neither does for everything), my tentative pick is the District of South Carolina (Fourth Circuit), but that preference is weak and unverified in its specifics.

1. Why one consolidated indictment is best. Section 1347 punishes each execution of the scheme (up to 10 years per count; 20 if serious bodily injury; life if death). Under USSG 1B1.3(a)(2), conduct that is part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan (same purpose and modus operandi, here false insurance claims from one practice) is counted as relevant conduct, so the loss from BOTH states' false claims can be aggregated under 2B1.1 in a single sentencing, and 3D1.2(d) groups the fraud counts. Where the guideline range exceeds the statutory maximum on any one count, 5G1.2(d) requires running counts consecutively to the extent needed to reach the total punishment, which is how a single multi-count indictment can produce more than 10 years. By contrast, if one district convicts first and the other later, 5G1.3(b) requires the second sentence to run concurrently with the undischarged term where that term resulted from offenses that were relevant conduct and increased the offense level, and 5G1.3(c)/(d) otherwise leaves concurrency/consecutiveness to the court with a strong tilt toward adjustment/concurrency. So split prosecutions risk concurrent time and a first sentence that already counted the other state's loss as relevant conduct. (I did not retrieve the full text of 5G1.3 or 5G1.2; these points rest on search summaries of the Guidelines, so they should be checked against the current Manual.)

2. Venue limits which office can do it. 18 U.S.C. 3237(a): an offense begun, continued or completed in more than one district may be prosecuted in any district where it was begun, continued, or completed. A single indictment covering both states is possible for one office only if the scheme or the individual claims touched that district (e.g., claims submitted to or processed by an insurer or contractor located there, payments received there). If the Georgia claims were purely local to the Southern District of Georgia and the South Carolina claims purely local to South Carolina, neither office can lawfully charge the other state's claims, and the offices would need separate indictments (with the 5G1.3 concurrency problem above) or a venue-proper third district. Venue is a factual predicate I could not resolve from the question.

3. Circuit-law differences if the choice is otherwise open. Loss under 2B1.1(b)(1) drives most of the range (plus a +2 to +4 enhancement under 2B1.1(b)(7) for federal health care offenses involving government programs with loss over $1M). Historically, the commentary defined loss as the greater of actual or intended loss. After Kisor, the Third Circuit (Banks, 55 F.4th 246) held loss means actual loss, and the Eleventh Circuit en banc (Dupree, 57 F.4th 1269) held commentary cannot expand an unambiguous guideline. One search summary reports the Fourth Circuit has reaffirmed intended loss post-Kisor, and another reports a more recent Fourth Circuit decision (Boler) reading 'loss' as actual loss in a tax context; I did not verify either. Effective Nov. 1, 2024, Amendment 827 moved the greater-of-actual-or-intended-loss rule into the guideline text, which largely eliminates the split for sentencing under the current Manual (subject to ex post facto limits if the conduct and the applicable Manual predate that amendment and Dupree-type reasoning applies in the Eleventh Circuit). Given the question assumes both judges follow the Guidelines, this difference is probably not decisive; at most it modestly favors South Carolina for older conduct.

4. Caveats. Guidelines are advisory (Booker); the statutory maximum per count caps each sentence; the amount of loss in each state, venue facts, criminal history, and ex post facto/Manual-version issues are not given. I could not access ussc.gov primary text directly (blocked), so Guidelines propositions rest on search-result summaries, not verified primary text.

claims.text: The office that can lawfully charge all conduct from both states in one indictment should do so; consolidation maximizes exposure via aggregated relevant-conduct loss and 5G1.2(d) stacking, whereas separate prosecutions risk concurrent sentences under 5G1.3.
Venue under 3237(a) depends on facts (where claims were submitted/processed); if each state's claims are purely local, neither office can charge all conduct.
Circuit law on intended vs actual loss is a secondary tiebreaker, largely mooted by Amendment 827 for current-Manual sentencing.
